messages.subject: Initialization failed using welton model
parts:
Dear list,
I'm totally new at using stan and i would like to use it  for my simulation study.
As far as I know, the model is correct, and i get results for some values, but for others values i get the message
Initialization failed after 100 attempts.  Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the model.
error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done
I really don't know what i have to do now, should i specify initial values (i'm not totally sure of the impact), or is my model wrongly written ?
I join my model, and an exemple of the R code thats calls it.
The model i'm trying to use is presented here http://www.bris.ac.uk/cmm/research/rss-group/welton.pdf
Any help will be greatly appreciated, to correct or just to understand my errors
Thanks!

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Initialization failed using welton model
parts:
What's happening is that Stan can't find reasonable starting
values that don't lead to -infinity or NaN values in the first
few iterations.



1. The dealbreaker as far as model correctness is that you
need the constraints declared for variables to match the support of
their sampling distributions.

Your declaration

real<lower=0> s_d[J];

is not compatible with the sampling statement

s_d[m]~uniform(0,2);

The declaration needs to be:

real<lower=0,upper=2> s_d[J];


I verified this fixed the problem using your code and everything
converges quickly and has a high effective sample size per iteration.


2. Because you're going to use meta this as an index
for d[J], you really want the constraint to be declared as

int<lower=1,upper=J> meta[K];

This makes the intent clearer and can catch potential errors in data input.


3. Given that x is a binary integer variable, it's more
efficient to code this

theta_0[i]<-d[meta[i]]+beta[i]*x[i];

as:

theta_0[i] <- d[meta[i]];
if (x[i])
theta_0[i] <- theta_0[i] + beta[i];

Also, you can make theta_0 a local variable in the loop.

I can see you're bringing in BUGS programming idioms :-)


4. It's MUCH more efficient to vectorize.

You can do this for every one of your sampling statements.
For example, rather than

for (m in 1:J){
d[m]~normal(0,1000);

write just

d ~ normal(0,1000);

And rather than

for (i in 1:K){
...
y[i]~normal(theta[i],sigma[i]);

you can pull this out of the loop and write just:

y ~ normal(theta, sigma);

You can even define a local s_d_meta variable, assign to
it, and call, which will be more efficient, but a bit ugly, e.g.,

real s_d_meta[K];
for (k in 1:K)
s_d_meta[k] <- s_d[meta[k]];

and then replace

theta[i]~normal(theta_0[i],s_d[meta[i]]);

with

theta ~ normal(theta_0, s_d_meta);

Allocations and loops with assignment are essentially free in Stan
compared to sampling statements, and vectorized sampling statements
are much faster.

Having said all this, get the model working to your satisfaction first!


5. At the risk of sounding like a broken record on the list, are you really
expecting d to take on values like 2000? If not, a tighter prior will
improve inference computationally.

6. From the powerpoint, what did you mean that inverse_gamma(0.001, 0.001)
priors performed best? What else did you try?


For reference, here's the model with some indentation (Stan emacs mode is
awesome!).


data{
int<lower=0> J;
int<lower=0> K;
int<lower=0> meta[K];
int<lower=0,upper=1> x[K];
real y[K];
real<lower=0> sigma[K];
}
parameters{
real b0;
real<lower=0> s_phi;
real<lower=0> s_kappa;
real<lower=0> s_d[J];
real b[J];
real d[J];
real theta[K];
real beta[K];
}
model{
real theta_0[K];
for (m in 1:J){
d[m]~normal(0,1000);
s_d[m]~uniform(0,2);
}
b0~normal(0,1000);
s_phi~uniform(0,2);
s_kappa~uniform(0,2);

for (m in 1:J)
b[m]~normal(b0,s_phi);

for (i in 1:K){
beta[i]~normal(b[meta[i]],s_kappa);
theta_0[i]<-d[meta[i]]+beta[i]*x[i];
theta[i]~normal(theta_0[i],s_d[meta[i]]);
y[i]~normal(theta[i],sigma[i]);
}
}

- Bob

I'd get it working first, then worry about optimization
if it's not fast enough. There are advantages to having
a clean, readable model spec, namely less of a chance to introduce
subtle errors in the code and a model that you can explain to
people and expand more easily.

- Bob
